summary: Woodford pressed doctrinal harm and non-Christian moral goods; Scrivener answered through Christian anthropology, reforming institutions, sacred equality, and nonviolent interpretation.

pro.text: They are murdering their children. That's bad.
pro.context: Woodford isolates the alleged contradiction between condemning child sacrifice and commanding lethal collective punishment.

con.text: to enslave an image of God is as unthinkable
con.context: Scrivener grounds categorical opposition to enslavement in the universal status conferred by divine image-bearing.

pro-prior-human-decency.words: Human compassion, love, hope, and decency exist before religious institutions, which appropriate those goods while adding doctrines, dogmas, and revelations capable of poisoning them.
pro-prior-human-decency.critique: Strongest feature: The memorable well metaphor establishes an intelligible motion-level framework by separating antecedent human compassion from subsequently introduced doctrinal commitments and institutionalized religious authority. Principal limitation: Its categorical chronology and universal terminology remain insufficiently qualified, while the illustrative metaphor cannot independently demonstrate that religion merely appropriates humane capacities or contributes only contamination. Live burden: The case must provide representative comparative evidence showing that independently available human decency adequately explains acknowledged religious benefits while specific authoritative additions generate avoidable, materially consequential harms. Locked score: The supplied strong/competent band reflects excellent relevance and a readily recoverable governing proposition, moderated by underdeveloped causal substantiation, unstable scope, missing qualification, and limited engagement with narrower accounts of distinctive religious contribution.

pro-unique-good-without-harm-test.words: Religion fails the proposed poison test unless it contributes something uniquely good without simultaneously introducing a significant doctrinal or institutional harm.
pro-unique-good-without-harm-test.critique: Strongest feature: The move formulates a lucid, falsifiable challenge that organizes the subsequent exchange and gives the opposing side an immediately understandable route for presenting distinctive religious benefits. Principal limitation: The uniqueness-without-harm conjunction is exceptionally demanding and remains undefended as the motion's necessary standard, excluding mixed, comparative, or indispensable contributions through an unacknowledged threshold choice. Live burden: The argument must justify why any accompanying bad defeats a genuinely distinctive good, specify the relevant religious universe, and explain why net effects or counterfactual necessity are insufficient alternatives. Locked score: The supplied strong/competent band recognizes outstanding motion relevance, clarity, and argumentative usefulness while incorporating materially overstated necessity, incomplete scope control, modest evidentiary warrant, and an insufficiently charitable representation of the strongest opposing position.

tags.label: Begging the question
tags.context: The proposed test partially embeds the disputed conclusion by requiring a uniquely good contribution accompanied by no bad consequence.

con-internal-critique-corrupt-religion.words: Christian scripture distinguishes self-exalting religion from outward blessing and supplies prophets, institutional separations, and Christ-centered standards for criticizing corrupt religious power.
con-internal-critique-corrupt-religion.critique: Strongest feature: The scriptural contrasts between inward self-exaltation, outward blessing, separated offices, and prophetic confrontation supply a coherent internal mechanism for criticizing rather than merely protecting religious authority. Principal limitation: Selected canonical examples establish the availability of internal criticism but do not demonstrate its representativeness, historical effectiveness, uniqueness, or capacity to outweigh the harms identified elsewhere. Live burden: The response must connect these interpretive resources to dependable institutional correction and show why their religious derivation matters beyond the ordinary possibility that traditions contain both criticism and corruption. Locked score: The supplied strong/competent band reflects clear recoverability, good warrant, measured calibration, and charitable contact with an undifferentiated poison thesis, while preserving the unresolved distinction between internal self-criticism and distinctive net benefit.

con-devotion-compassion-institutions.words: Christian devotion redirected service toward neighbors as divine images and helped generate care institutions and reforms opposing infanticide, pederasty, and gladiatorial violence.
con-devotion-compassion-institutions.critique: Strongest feature: The move supplies both a theological mechanism and concrete institutional outcomes, directly connecting service to Jesus with neighbor care, exposed-infant protection, and opposition to entrenched violence. Principal limitation: Its categorical claims of uniquely Christian authorship and abolition outrun the comparative historical evidence presented, leaving chronology, causation, independent precedents, and non-Christian participation substantially unexamined. Live burden: The case must distinguish originating compassion from organizing or amplifying it, document the asserted causal pathway, and compare relevant societies sufficiently to support distinctiveness rather than consequential participation. Locked score: The supplied strong/competent band recognizes direct burden contact, coherent mechanism, memorable examples, and a serious answer to appropriation, while incorporating missing qualifications, limited comparative substantiation, overstated exclusivity, and incomplete treatment of ordinary human-compassion explanations.

con-human-poison-christian-antidote.words: Pride, violence, and domination characterize humanity across religious and secular movements, while Christianity supplies standards for condemning that poison and presents Jesus as its antidote.
con-human-poison-christian-antidote.critique: Strongest feature: The response directly contests religion-specific causation by placing ideological atrocities within a broader human pattern and then offers the crucified victim of religious violence as a Christian corrective. Principal limitation: The sweeping comparative claim that secular causes killed far more lacks adequate substantiation, while locating violence generally in humanity does not exclude religion as a distinctive amplifier or legitimating mechanism. Live burden: The reply must separate baseline human viciousness from marginal religious effects and demonstrate how the proposed Christian antidote reliably constrains adherents, institutions, and authoritative interpretations in practice. Locked score: The supplied strong/competent band reflects strong relevance, a recoverable diagnostic challenge, and a powerful thematic reversal, moderated by materially overstated comparison, unstable terminology, weak comparative evidence, and incomplete contact with the additive-harm thesis.

pro-community-with-doctrinal-subordinati.words: Religious community and charity carry doctrinal costs when authoritative teachings subordinate women's testimony and religious institutions impose grave harms on gay people.
pro-community-with-doctrinal-subordinati.critique: Strongest feature: The move grants genuine community and charitable activity before identifying concrete doctrinal costs, thereby answering claimed religious benefit without denying observable goods or relying on blanket dismissal. Principal limitation: Particular Islamic teachings and violent practices are extended toward religion generally without enough representativeness, doctrinal-attribution, jurisdictional, or causal analysis to establish the breadth of the conclusion. Live burden: The argument must show that the cited harms arise authoritatively and characteristically from the relevant religion, accompany the claimed goods counterfactually, and are not separable abuses or localized interpretations. Locked score: The supplied strong/competent band rewards its fair concession, vivid evidence, logical fit, and direct application of the governing poison test while preserving limitations in generalization, comparative support, scope qualification, and proof that every relevant community carries equivalent costs.

pro-community-is-human-not-unique.words: Community exists in secular settings and is therefore a reproducible human good rather than an exclusively or generically unique contribution of religion.
pro-community-is-human-not-unique.critique: Strongest feature: The concise secular-community counterexample soundly defeats the generic proposition that community as such belongs exclusively to religion, while preserving the acknowledged value of communal belonging. Principal limitation: The reply compresses the opposing claim from distinctive devotional formation and historically consequential institutions into simple community existence, leaving specific religious motives, forms, scope, and effects substantially unanswered. Live burden: The argument must compare secular and religious communities at the level actually disputed and determine whether Christianity uniquely shaped outward service, enemy concern, institutional durability, or humanitarian expansion. Locked score: The supplied strong/competent band reflects stable terminology, proportionate calibration, clear logical force, and effective contact with generic uniqueness, tempered by only partial responsiveness and insufficient engagement with narrower historical-causal claims about Christian community.

pro-christian-dominion-failed-to-abolish.words: Centuries of Christian political dominance created ample opportunities to prohibit slavery, yet Christian authorities did not categorically reject ownership of human beings.
pro-christian-dominion-failed-to-abolish.critique: Strongest feature: The argument converts prolonged Christian political power into a forceful historical test of claimed humanitarian causation, asking what authoritative doctrine accomplished when institutions possessed governing capacity. Principal limitation: The fifteen-century formulation compresses substantial regional, jurisdictional, theological, and institutional variation, while the excerpt supplies no representative chronology comparing opportunities, constraints, reforms, and contrary authorities. Live burden: The reply must document where categorical abolition was practicable, distinguish delayed influence from complete ineffectiveness, and explain why prolonged coexistence with slavery outweighs eventual Christian abolitionist reasoning. Locked score: The supplied strong/competent band recognizes powerful causal relevance, direct contact with institutional-fruit and antidote claims, and a clear counterfactual challenge, moderated by broad historical compression, limited supporting detail, unstable political scope, and incomplete treatment of gradualist alternatives.

con-original-sin-precedes-religion.words: Pride, domination, brutality, and violence precede later religious institutions, undermining an unpoisoned human baseline while leaving Christianity available as a corrective standard.
con-original-sin-precedes-religion.critique: Strongest feature: The ancient-world references and qualified historical language directly challenge the opening metaphor's chronology by showing that brutality and domination are embedded in humanity rather than introduced only afterward. Principal limitation: Defeating an innocent baseline does not defeat the narrower claim that doctrines can intensify, legitimize, organize, or perpetuate independently existing human vices in distinctive ways. Live burden: The response must compare religion's marginal causal contribution against secular mechanisms and connect Christian anthropology to a demonstrated corrective effect rather than merely relocating the original source of wrongdoing. Locked score: The supplied strong/competent band reflects excellent diagnostic responsiveness, appropriate calibration, concrete historical orientation, and strong central-bridge contact, while preserving compressed categories, incomplete answers to uniqueness and slavery, and insufficient engagement with additive religious harm.

con-monogamy-constrains-male-power.words: Christian monogamous marriage constrained elite male sexual access and aggression, offering women and children meaningful protection within family and social arrangements.
con-monogamy-constrains-male-power.critique: Strongest feature: The move identifies a concrete institutional mechanism through which Christian sexual teaching could restrict exploitative elite male power and materially benefit women and children. Principal limitation: Its categorical protective description lacks historical, comparative, class, and jurisdictional qualification, and one beneficial mechanism cannot establish the overall effects of a broader doctrinal system that may also subordinate women. Live burden: The response must document counterfactual improvements attributable to Christian monogamy, compare alternative family regimes, and weigh constrained male access against restrictions imposed upon women's agency, testimony, and status. Locked score: The supplied strong/competent band recognizes coherent mechanism, direct responsiveness, clear proposition recovery, and substantial relevance to institutional fruits, while incorporating limited empirical support, overstated certainty, incomplete scope control, and unresolved coexistence between protection and subordination.

pro-humane-motif-retreats-from-scripture.words: Humane Christian defenses of women retreat from explicit restrictive texts and import compassion that those doctrines and revelations do not themselves supply.
pro-humane-motif-retreats-from-scripture.critique: Strongest feature: The contrast between explicit restrictive language and a humane presentation sharply diagnoses a possible interpretive retreat, directly pressuring claims that scripture itself generates the compassion used in its defense. Principal limitation: The response treats selective omission or canonical prioritization as wholesale removal from scripture, without comparing contextual readings, countertexts, theological synthesis, or internal principles supporting the humane motif. Live burden: The argument must establish that the relevant compassion is genuinely external rather than canonically derived and show that broader interpretation cannot responsibly constrain or reinterpret difficult passages from within Christianity. Locked score: The supplied strong/competent band rewards unusually direct responsiveness, clear textual tension, coherent consequence, and strong route completion, while retaining materially overstated necessity, reduced charity, broad treatment of scripture, and insufficient examination of whole-canon alternatives.

con-image-of-god-against-slavery.words: Enslaving a person made in God's image violates universal sacred status and humanity's vocation to exercise dominion rather than suffer ownership by others.
con-image-of-god-against-slavery.critique: Strongest feature: The inference from universal divine image-bearing to categorical opposition to enslavement is concise, morally powerful, internally coherent, and directly responsive to demands for a Christian doctrinal basis. Principal limitation: The accompanying historical assertion about abolition remains unsupported by specific actors, texts, mechanisms, or comparisons, and the move does not explain Christianity's long coexistence with slaveholding institutions. Live burden: The case must demonstrate how image-bearing became causally effective, why contrary Christian interpretations were mistaken on Christian grounds, and whether the doctrine was historically necessary rather than merely available. Locked score: The supplied very-strong band reflects exceptional logical clarity, stable formulation, central relevance, charitable qualification, and a genuine doctrinal answer, tempered by limited historical substantiation and an unresolved gap between normative resources and delayed institutional application.

con-trinitarian-ground-of-goodness.words: Trinitarian Christianity identifies goodness with God's eternal loving life, making evil a violation of the love that shapes creation rather than an arbitrary command.
con-trinitarian-ground-of-goodness.critique: Strongest feature: The Trinitarian account grounds love inside Christian doctrine rather than importing it externally, providing an elegant internal answer to arbitrary-command concerns and the alleged retreat from scripture. Principal limitation: Identifying God, goodness, and love risks redescribing rather than resolving the problem unless independent criteria connect divine nature to recognizable love and adjudicate apparently conflicting commands. Live burden: The account must explain how finite interpreters distinguish faithful revelation from moral misdescription and apply divine love consistently to conquest, slavery, subordination, punishment, and enemy concern. Locked score: The supplied very-strong band recognizes excellent diagnostic responsiveness, stable theological formulation, proportionate conditional reasoning, and direct central relevance, while retaining limited independent warrant, unresolved hard-case application, and the need to defend the asserted identities rather than presuppose them.

con-equality-and-gradual-abolition.words: Christianity established spiritual equality and eventually transformed that status into social abolition, with gradual reform avoiding destabilizing consequences of immediate emancipation.
con-equality-and-gradual-abolition.critique: Strongest feature: The reply combines an equality principle with a practical account of gradual institutional transformation, directly explaining how anti-slavery implications might precede safe and politically achievable abolition. Principal limitation: The gradualist explanation is asserted selectively and retrospectively, without evidence that immediate prohibition was broadly impossible or that scriptural accommodation actually accelerated rather than delayed emancipation. Live burden: The case must specify mechanisms translating spiritual equality into legal reform, compare feasible historical alternatives, and explain why explicit prohibitions addressed lesser practices while human ownership remained regulated. Locked score: The supplied strong/competent band reflects substantial responsiveness, coherent trajectory, useful attention to transition costs, and direct engagement with abolition, tempered by incomplete historical evidence, selective necessity claims, compressed causal chronology, and insufficient reconciliation of equality with prolonged Christian slaveholding.

pro-selective-gradualism-on-slavery.words: Appeals to gradual abolition appear selective because scripture explicitly prohibits other conduct while regulating rather than categorically forbidding ownership of human beings.
pro-selective-gradualism-on-slavery.critique: Strongest feature: The comparison with explicit prohibitions exposes a precise selectivity problem for gradualism, asking why divine accommodation was indispensable for slavery but unnecessary for other socially embedded conduct. Principal limitation: The analogy remains incomplete without comparing the transition costs, institutional dependencies, textual settings, and enforcement conditions of slavery with the other prohibited practices invoked. Live burden: The argument must establish that categorical prohibition was historically practicable, would not create equivalent harms, and is the expected form of guidance under the opponent's own account of revelation. Locked score: The supplied very-strong band recognizes sharp diagnostic contact, strong logical pressure, excellent burden relevance, and a clearly recoverable inconsistency test, while preserving limited comparative historical support, compressed contextual differences, and the need to distinguish regulation, toleration, reform trajectory, and endorsement.

con-enemy-love-beyond-tribe.words: Christian commands to love enemies and protect the weak extend moral concern beyond kin and tribe, giving socially costly compassion distinctive authority.
con-enemy-love-beyond-tribe.critique: Strongest feature: Enemy love supplies a genuinely demanding norm and a plausible mechanism for expanding moral concern beyond kinship, reciprocity, strength, status, and ordinary communal solidarity. Principal limitation: The categorical description of out-group compassion as unnatural exceeds the evolutionary and philosophical support offered and understates cross-cultural human capacities for costly concern beyond immediate affiliation. Live burden: The case must distinguish uniquely authoritative amplification from exclusive origination, document institutional consequences, and compare Christian enemy love with analogous norms and practices in other traditions. Locked score: The supplied strong/competent band reflects direct contact with the universal-compassion dispute, a clear scaling mechanism, meaningful doctrinal specificity, and considerable relevance, moderated by materially overstated naturalness claims, modest comparative evidence, reduced charity, and failure to answer the separate no-harm requirement.

pro-divine-nature-canaan-test.words: Commands attributed to God in the conquest narratives test whether identifying goodness with divine nature can make apparently atrocious killing and captivity morally acceptable.
pro-divine-nature-canaan-test.critique: Strongest feature: The concrete conquest example transforms an abstract divine-nature account into a demanding consistency test and directly connects sacred worth, love, revelation, killing, and moral recognizability. Principal limitation: The compressed paraphrase combines contested passages and interpretive claims, so its evidentiary force depends upon disputed questions about genre, hyperbole, combatants, collective judgment, and the treatment of captives. Live burden: The challenge must preserve its conditional structure while requiring the defense to show how the relevant text coheres with loving divine nature rather than merely invoking authority or canonical culmination. Locked score: The supplied very-strong band reflects exceptional relevance, coherent conditional reasoning, explicit qualification, and forceful engagement with the theological foundation, tempered by contested textual reconstruction and incomplete treatment of contextual alternatives.

con-objective-ground-beyond-agreement.words: Present social agreement cannot make slavery or caste objectively wrong, so moral condemnation requires reasons and foundations beyond contingent collective preference.
con-objective-ground-beyond-agreement.critique: Strongest feature: The pro-slavery-consensus hypothetical effectively demonstrates that numerical or social agreement alone cannot constitute objective moral truth and keeps the metaethical question visible beneath shared condemnation. Principal limitation: Refuting simple conventionalism does not establish Christian theism, because secular realism, constructivism, contractualism, reasons-based ethics, and other alternatives remain unaddressed, while objectivity's necessity is itself undefended. Live burden: The response must offer a positive foundation, compare it against credible non-Christian accounts, and show that its own treatment of conquest and slavery satisfies rather than merely asserts objective goodness. Locked score: The supplied mixed band reflects a clear proposition, useful diagnostic pressure, and legitimate subsidiary relevance, limited by partial responsiveness, narrowed representation of secular morality, insufficient positive warrant, and failure to resolve the concrete consistency challenge.

pro-nonchristian-moral-goods-test.words: Claims that modern moral goods require Christianity are testable against acknowledged contributions from non-Christian people, cultures, family practices, and ethical criticism.
pro-nonchristian-moral-goods-test.critique: Strongest feature: The falsification question elicits the opponent's own example of beneficial non-Christian family practices, creating unusually direct evidence against an exhaustive Christian-derivation or necessity claim. Principal limitation: One acknowledged contribution defeats exclusivity but does not determine the degree of Christian cultural influence, independent origin, counterfactual availability, or historical formation of the surrounding moral vocabulary. Live burden: The argument must distinguish participation from genuine causal independence and compare specific non-Christian goods with the narrower claim that Christianity substantially amplified or institutionalized universal concern. Locked score: The supplied very-strong band reflects excellent diagnostic responsiveness, stable scope, matched calibration, strong warrant, and charitable handling of a testable causal claim, while retaining an unresolved question about deeper cultural dependence and the separate metaethical grounding dispute.

con-conquest-context-and-christian-prohi.words: Ancient military hyperbole and judgment context qualify conquest narratives, while their culmination in the crucified Christ prohibits Christians from violently enforcing divine justice.
con-conquest-context-and-christian-prohi.critique: Strongest feature: The response offers multiple interpretive resources and concludes with an unequivocal Christian prohibition on violent enforcement, directly addressing textual meaning, canonical development, and contemporary religious conduct. Principal limitation: The selected evidence most clearly supports the later nonviolence claim, while hyperbole, combatant limitation, exceptional judgment, and historical consistency receive insufficient demonstration to vindicate the narrated events. Live burden: The defense must show precisely what the conquest texts affirm, explain remaining collective violence, and establish that Christ-centered culmination resolves rather than bypasses the moral character of earlier divine authorization. Locked score: The supplied strong/competent band recognizes comprehensive contact, coherent canonical reasoning, strong relevance, careful qualification, and charitable engagement, while preserving evidentiary gaps, compressed genre claims, and tension between present prohibition and past judgment.

pro-child-sacrifice-punishment-incoheren.words: Condemning a culture for child sacrifice cannot coherently justify commanding the killing of its children or taking its young girls as captives.
pro-child-sacrifice-punishment-incoheren.critique: Strongest feature: The response isolates a devastating normative mismatch: opposition to child sacrifice cannot itself justify killing the endangered children, making the residual moral issue exceptionally clear and immediate. Principal limitation: Its force depends upon the contested literal premise that the relevant commands include indiscriminate child killing, yet the move states that premise categorically despite the opponent's immediate interpretive denial. Live burden: The argument must establish or explicitly condition upon the textual scope, while requiring any alternative reading to explain apparently comprehensive language and the treatment of noncombatants without evasion. Locked score: The supplied very-strong band reflects outstanding logical coherence, decisive responsiveness, direct doctrinal-harm relevance, and proportionate reasoning given its premises, tempered by disputed textual warrant, incomplete qualification, and reduced charity toward contextual alternatives.

newArguments.title: The correction-cost test
newArguments.text: A useful comparison asks not merely whether religious communities perform good acts, but what happens when their authoritative claims conflict with evidence of harm. If revelation, sacred status, or institutional loyalty raises the social and psychological cost of revision, religion adds a distinctive correction burden even when believers remain compassionate. The relevant evidence would compare how quickly similarly situated religious and secular institutions acknowledge victims, revise rules, and permit dissent. This test avoids claiming that religion originates every vice; it asks whether particular authority structures make preventable harms unusually persistent.

novelty.explanation: This is a new institutional test focused on revision costs rather than the transcript's uniqueness or historical-origin tests.

newArguments.title: Counterfactual benefit accounting
newArguments.text: Claims of distinctive religious benefit should be evaluated counterfactually: would the institution, reform, or norm probably have emerged without the disputed doctrine, and did that doctrine also impose measurable costs? Christian participation in abolition or care can be historically important without proving exclusive causation. Conversely, non-Christian parallels do not erase Christian influence. A balanced inquiry compares timing, independent emergence, diffusion, resistance, and opportunity costs. If humane outcomes repeatedly track shared human concern while harmful restrictions track revelation-specific commitments, the comparative pattern supports the affirmative without requiring the implausible claim that religion contributes nothing good.

novelty.explanation: This introduces an explicit causal-accounting framework that neither participant fully articulated in the live exchange.

newArguments.title: Moral technology and transmission
newArguments.text: A moral insight can be naturally available yet socially fragile. Christianity's possible distinctiveness may lie less in inventing compassion than in packaging equal worth, enemy love, confession, and care into narratives, rituals, offices, and translocal communities capable of transmitting demanding norms across generations. That claim is empirically testable through institutional diffusion, durability, and reform language. It also concedes non-Christian virtue. If Christian structures repeatedly helped costly concern survive beyond charismatic individuals and local kin groups, they supplied a meaningful contribution even though the underlying human capacity was never exclusively Christian.

novelty.explanation: This introduces a transmission-centered account of religious contribution distinct from claims of exclusive moral invention.

newArguments.title: Internal contradiction as reform leverage
newArguments.text: A tradition's inconsistency can sometimes strengthen internal reform: abolitionists may confront slaveholding Christians not with an alien ethic but with the contradiction between universal image-bearing and human ownership. Internal arguments can mobilize adherents, redirect institutions, and deny defenders an easy claim that criticism is merely external hostility. This does not excuse delay or prove that doctrine caused every reform. It identifies a practical mechanism by which sacred commitments become leverage against entrenched practice. The historical question is then comparative: when and how effectively did reformers use those commitments, and what competing interpretations obstructed them?

novelty.explanation: This is a new mechanism explaining how doctrinal inconsistency can enable rather than merely discredit internal reform.
